x: Start here AI 101 for beginners New to AI? This is a plain-English starter course: what it is, why businesses use it, how to ask it for what you want, and how to stay safe. Time: about 45 to 60 minutes on your own, or use it with the facilitator guide for a group. No coding, no experience and no payment needed. Tool plans and limits change, so check each tool's official site for what is free today. The 30-second version AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are very fast assistants that predict useful text, images or answers from patterns they learned. They are great at first drafts, summaries and brainstorming. They can also be confidently wrong, so a person checks the result and stays responsible for it. What AI actually is Business view: think of a very fast new hire who has read a huge amount, never gets tired, but sometimes makes things up and does not know your company. You would give that person clear instructions, check their work and keep private files locked away. That is how to treat AI. A little more technical: a chatbot is built on a large language model (LLM). During training it studied enormous amounts of text and learned which words tend to follow which. When you type a prompt , it predicts a helpful reply one piece at a time. It is not looking things up unless the tool has a search feature, and it does not truly "know" whether something is true. That is why it can produce a wrong answer in a very confident tone, called a hallucination . Why businesses use it Time: first drafts of emails, reports and ad copy in minutes instead of an hour. Cost: small teams can do work that used to need an agency or an extra hire. Sorting and summarizing: turn long documents, reviews or call notes into short summaries. Ideas: get ten options fast, then pick and improve the best one. What AI is good at, and where it struggles Usually good at Be careful with First drafts and rewrites Exact facts, names, quotes and sources Summarizing long text you give it Math and numbers without a calculator or spreadsheet Brainstorming options Recent events, unless the tool searches the web Explaining a topic in plain words Legal, medical and financial decisions Sorting and labeling lots of text Anything private or regulated How to write a good prompt A weak prompt gets a weak answer. Use these five parts, in any order: Role: who should the AI act as? ("a friendly small-business marketing coach") Task: what exactly do you want? ("write three subject lines") Context: what does it need to know? (audience, goal, tone, anything it should avoid) Format: how should the answer look? ("a numbered list, under 100 words") Check: ask it to flag what to verify, or to ask you questions first. Copy Act as a friendly small-business marketing coach. Write three subject lines for an email announcing our Thursday workshop for college students. Keep each under 8 words, no hype, no emojis. Then tell me which one you would test first and why. If the first answer is not right, just reply with what to change. Talking back and forth is normal and is how most people get good results. Your first hour: four short exercises Open any free AI chat tool. Use made-up or non-private information only. Copy a prompt, run it, then read the answer critically. Exercise 1: Ask for a plain-English explanation (5 minutes) Pick something you have always found confusing, such as a term from class or work. Copy Explain [topic] to me like I am new to it. Use one everyday example from a small business. Then give me three questions I could ask to check I understood. Exercise 2: Turn messy notes into something clean (5 minutes) Type or paste a few made-up or non-private bullet points. Do not use real client or personal details. Copy Turn these notes into a short, friendly follow-up email. Keep it under 120 words and end with one clear next step. Notes: - met Tuesday - they liked the proposal - need pricing by Friday Exercise 3: Make it check itself (5 minutes) Ask a factual question about something you already know well, so you can spot mistakes. Copy Answer this question, then list which parts of your answer I should double-check and why: [your question] Exercise 4: Use AI as a coach, not a ghostwriter (5 minutes) Paste a paragraph you wrote yourself. Copy Act as a friendly editor. Point out the three biggest improvements for clarity, and explain each one. Do not rewrite the whole paragraph. Stay safe from day one I did not paste client names, health details, account numbers or passwords. I checked any fact, number or date I plan to rely on. I read the result myself before sending it to anyone. I know my school or workplace rules about AI use, and I follow them. The full checklist is on Using AI safely . Check yourself Try to answer each question first, then open it. 1. An AI chatbot gives you a confident answer with a statistic. What should you do before using it in a client email? Best answer: Check the number against an official or original source. AI can state wron

Club guide Quick demo Your browser cannot play this video. Illustrated walkthrough of a scheduled news watch. It is not a screen recording of any tool. What it is A scheduled task is an alarm clock for an AI. Instead of you opening a chat each morning and asking "what is new in AI?", you write the request once and the AI runs it by itself at a set time, then leaves you a summary. Think of it as a personal research assistant who reads the news before you wake up. Why people use it Keeps you current on a topic without spending an hour scrolling. Businesses use the same idea for competitor monitoring, regulation tracking and market news. It turns one good prompt into a repeating habit. This is the simplest form of an AI workflow . Pick your tool Google Alerts (free, no AI): at google.com/alerts, enter a keyword and Google emails you new web results daily or weekly. Good for brand and name tracking. It lists links but does not summarize. Muse (Meta): reports say its private cloud computer can run recurring jobs and keep working after you close the app. See the Muse guide and check the app for how scheduling works for you. Claude scheduled tasks: in Claude you can create a task that runs on a schedule with its own prompt. Check your plan and settings for availability and limits, and note that some tasks only run while the desktop app is open. ChatGPT Tasks and similar: several chat assistants offer scheduled prompts. Availability depends on the plan, so check the app. Start free: set up Google Alerts first (5 minutes). Add an AI summary task when you know which topics are worth your time. How to get started Choose one topic. Five topics in one summary becomes noise. Choose how often: daily for fast-moving topics like AI, weekly for slow ones like regulation. Pick the delivery spot: an email draft, a notification, or the task's own results page. Copy a prompt below and edit the brackets. Run it once by hand and read the result. Fix anything that is too long, too vague, or missing sources. Turn on the schedule. Review after one week and cut what you did not read. Prompts to copy Daily AI news Copy You are my news researcher. Search the web for NEW items from the last 24 hours (go back 3 days only if nothing new turns up) about: 1) major AI model or product launches, 2) AI laws and regulation, 3) new AI tools worth learning. Skip rumors and old news. For each item give: a one-sentence summary in your own words, why it matters for a business student, and a link to the original source. Start with a 2-sentence top takeaway. Keep it under 400 words. If nothing important happened, say so in one line. Weekly Medicare and insurance changes Copy Every Monday morning, search for changes in the last 7 days to Medicare Advantage, Medicare Supplement and ACA marketplace rules, CMS announcements, and carrier news in Utah. Use official sources (cms.gov, medicare.gov, state insurance department) first. List each change with the date, a plain-English summary, and the source link. Mark anything that affects what I tell clients as 'VERIFY BEFORE USE'. Do not give advice; only report what the sources say. Weekly club meeting ideas Copy Every Wednesday, find 5 new things related to AI that would make a good 2-minute talk at Thursday's club meeting: a new tool, a surprising use case, a business story, a risk or lawsuit, a student-friendly project. For each give the headline, two sentences on why it is interesting, and the source link. Rank them by how well they would spark discussion. Competitor or keyword watch Copy Each day, check for news about [COMPANY OR COMPETITOR] and [KEYWORD]. Report only what is new since yesterday: product changes, funding, hiring, pricing, customer complaints, legal issues. For each item add the source link and a one-line 'so what' for a small business. If there is nothing new, reply 'No news today.' Write a prompt that works Say how recent: "last 24 hours" beats "latest." Demand sources: a link for every item, so you can check it. Set a length: "under 400 words" keeps it readable. Add a no-news rule: otherwise the AI may invent filler. Say what to skip: rumors, old news, duplicates. Safety rules Open the sources. AI summaries can be wrong. Never act on a summary alone, especially for regulations, money or client advice. Keep it read-only. Tell the task not to send emails or change files unless you approve. No private data. Do not put client names or health details in a scheduled prompt. Web pages can contain tricks. Hidden text on a page may try to give your AI orders (prompt injection). This is another reason to keep tasks read-only. Watch your usage. Each run uses your plan's allowance. Start with one task. Teach others Facilitator guide: teach AI 101 in one hour Everything you need to run a beginner AI session for the club, a class or a workplace group, with no expert knowledge required. A ready-to-run guide for a one-hour beginner session. It works for the club, a class, a family group or a workplace lunch. Nothing here requires you to be an expert, only that you try the exercises yourself first. Before the session Read AI 101 for beginners and do all four exercises yourself. Pick one free AI chat tool and make sure you can sign in. Have a backup tool ready in case one is down. Prepare one example where AI is right and one where it is confidently wrong. Test them the same day, because answers change. Check the room: screen or projector, Wi-Fi, and a way to show this site. Have the QR code ready so people can open this site on their own device. Tell people to bring a phone or laptop. Make sure no one has to pay for anything. Decide how you will collect quick feedback at the end (a show of hands, sticky notes, or a message in the club chat). One-hour agenda Time Segment What to do 0:00 to 0:05 Welcome and warm-up Ask: "Raise a hand if you have used an AI chat tool. Now keep it up if you trust every answer." Most hands go down. Say what the session is: a safe, no-experience-needed hour. Ask people to rate their confidence with AI from 1 to 5 by a show of hands, and remember the rough result. 0:05 to 0:15 What AI is (the new-hire idea) Teach the 30-second version from AI 101 . Use the fast-new-hire comparison. Show one live example of AI being right and one of it being confidently wrong, so people see both. 0:15 to 0:25 Writing a good prompt Walk through Role, Task, Context, Format, Check. Run the marketing-coach prompt live, then change one part (the format, say) and show how the answer changes. 0:25 to 0:45 Hands-on exercises Pairs run Exercises 1 to 4 from AI 101 (about 5 minutes each). Walk the room. Remind everyone: made-up or non-private information only. Ask pairs to note one answer they would double-check. 0:45 to 0:52 Safety and honesty Use the paste checker on Using AI safely . Ask the group to guess the answer for two or three examples before you reveal it. 0:52 to 0:58 Questions and what is next Take questions (see the tough-questions list below). Point to Start here, the prompt library and the tool guides. 0:58 to 1:00 Feedback Repeat the 1 to 5 confidence check by show of hands. Ask for one thing that was useful and one thing to change, on sticky notes or aloud. Thank them. Short on time? For 30 minutes, keep the welcome, the new-hire idea, the prompt formula and two exercises. For 90 minutes, add the full safety checker and let pairs build their own prompt for a real, non-private task. Running the hands-on part Pair people up. Beginners learn faster when one person types and the other reads the answer critically, then they swap. Normalize wrong answers. When a tool gets something wrong, celebrate it as the lesson, not a failure. Keep data fake. Say it out loud at the start: made-up or non-private information only. Go at the slowest pace comfortably. It is better that everyone finishes two exercises than that a few finish four. Offer paper. Print the exercise prompts for anyone who prefers it. The page has a print view that hides the menus. Answering tough questions You do not need perfect answers. Being honest about what is uncertain builds trust. Will AI take my job? Be honest: nobody knows exactly. Some tasks will change, and people who can use AI well and check its work will be in demand. Point to the AI by industry page to show how work is shifting in different fields. Avoid promising either way. Is it cheating to use AI in school? It depends on the course and school. Tell people to read the syllabus and ask the instructor. Using AI to explain, quiz or coach is often treated differently from submitting AI-written work as your own. When in doubt, ask first and say how you used it. Can I trust what it says? Not blindly. Repeat the key habit: check names, numbers, dates and sources, and keep a person responsible for what goes out. Is my data safe? Policies differ by tool and plan and change over time. Tell people to read the tool's current data settings and to keep private information out unless their organization has approved the tool. Which tool should I use? Start with whichever free chat tool they can access. The goal is the skill, which transfers between tools. Plans and free limits change, so send people to each tool's official page. Make it welcoming Do not assume anyone's background. Explain every term the first time, and point to the glossary . Let people pass on any exercise without explaining why. Avoid hype and fear. The tone is curious and practical. Be mindful of accessibility: read slides aloud, use large text, and share the links so people can follow on their own device. API Application Programming Interface A set of rules that lets one program ask another program to do something. Like a waiter: you order from the menu, the kitchen does the work. Businesses use APIs to plug tools together (for example, an app calling FLUX to make a video). Example: send a prompt to an AI model's API and get a video back.

API key A secret password that identifies you to an API and tracks your usage and bill. Never paste it into public code or a GitHub repo. Store it in an environment variable or a .env file that is not committed.

CLI Command-Line Interface A way to control a program by typing text commands instead of clicking. Faster to repeat and easy to automate. Example: git status , or running Claude Code in your terminal.
GUI Graphical User Interface The click-and-drag version of a tool, like CapCut's editor.

MCP Model Context Protocol A standard that lets an AI assistant safely connect to outside tools and data (Gmail, Notion, calendars, databases). Think of it as a universal plug for AI. Example: a Higgsfield or Notion connector inside Claude.
Connector A ready-made link between an AI assistant and an app, often built on MCP.
SDK Software Development Kit A toolbox of pre-written code that makes an API easier to use in a language like Python.
LLM Large Language Model An AI trained on huge amounts of text that can write, summarize, and reason. Claude, GPT and Gemini are LLMs.
Model The trained AI itself. Different models are good at different things (text, images, video, audio).
Prompt The instructions you give an AI. Clear prompts (goal, context, format, constraints) get better results.
Token A small chunk of text an LLM reads or writes. Pricing and limits are often counted in tokens.
Context window How much text a model can keep in mind at once.
Agent AI agent An AI that can plan steps and use tools to finish a task, not just answer one question.
Workflow A repeatable chain of steps (sometimes called a stack). Example: dictate, generate, edit, publish.
Open weights / open source A model whose trained files are public so you can download and run it. License rules still apply, so check before using commercially. Many are on Hugging Face.
Fine-tuning Extra training of an existing model on your own examples so it fits your task.
LoRA Low-Rank Adaptation A cheap way to fine-tune a big model by training a small add-on instead of the whole thing.
Inference Using a trained model to produce an answer. This is what you pay for when you generate.
GPU Graphics Processing Unit The chip that does the heavy math for AI. Renting GPUs is a major AI cost.
Edge AI / on-device AI Running AI on your phone or laptop instead of a remote server. Better privacy and speed. Example: Google AI Edge Eloquent.
Cloud Computers you rent over the internet (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure).
Git Software that tracks changes to files so you can undo mistakes and collaborate.
GitHub A website that hosts Git projects (repositories) so people can share and work together.
Repo Repository A project folder tracked by Git. This site is one.
Commit A saved snapshot of your changes with a message.
Pull request (PR) A proposal to merge your changes into a project, reviewed by others.
GitHub Pages Free hosting that turns a repo into a website. This site uses it.
README The front-page file of a repo explaining what it is and how to use it.
SQL Structured Query Language The language for asking questions of a database.
Database Organized storage for business data (customers, sales, inventory).
JSON A simple text format for passing data between programs.
Prompt injection A trick where hidden text in a webpage or file tries to give an AI new instructions. Treat outside content as data, not commands.
Hallucination When an AI states something false with confidence. Always verify important facts.
GEO / AEO Generative / Answer Engine Optimization Making your business easy for AI assistants to find and recommend, like SEO for AI answers.
SEO Search Engine Optimization Improving your site so it ranks higher in search results.

404 page Error 404 The page a website shows when the address you asked for does not exist. A good one explains what happened and links back to useful pages. Code 404 means 'not found'. Example: this site's 404 page appears if you mistype a link.

Sitemap A file (sitemap.xml) that lists every page on a website so search engines can find them all. Like a table of contents for Google. Example: this site's sitemap lists the home page, every tool guide and more.
robots.txt A small file that tells search engines which parts of a site they may visit and where the sitemap is.

Open Graph (link preview) OG Hidden tags in a page that control the title, description and picture shown when you share its link in chats and social apps. Example: the card you see when you paste a link in GroupMe or LinkedIn.
Meta description A one-sentence summary in a page's code. Search engines often show it under the page title in results.
Static website A site made of ready-made files (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) with no server-side program. Fast, cheap or free to host, and easy to secure. This club site is one.
Fork Your own copy of someone else's GitHub repo. You can change it freely without touching the original. Example: fork the club repo, then edit your copy.
Branch A side version of a project where you can try changes without affecting the main version.
Merge Accepting a change and combining it into the main version of the project.
Progressive web app (PWA) PWA A website that can be installed on your phone or computer and opens like an app, without an app store. Example: this site can be added to your home screen.

PII Personally Identifiable Information Details that can identify a person, such as a name with contact information, an ID or account number, or health details. Keep it out of AI tools unless the tool is approved for it.
Kanban board A board with columns such as Ideas, In progress and Done. Cards move left to right so everyone can see the status of work. Example: the club roadmap board.
Break-even point The point where the savings from a choice equal its cost. After that, you come out ahead. Example: how many videos per month before an AI subscription costs less than the old way.

UI User Interface Everything a person sees and touches on a screen: buttons, menus, colors, text and layout. Good UI looks clear and is easy to use. Example: the Install app button and the search box on this site.

UX User Experience How easy, fast and pleasant it feels to get something done with a product, from first click to finish. UI is the look, and UX is the whole journey. Example: if finding the meeting time takes one tap, that is good UX.
Wireframe A simple black-and-white sketch of a page layout that shows where things go before any design or code. Cheap to change.
Prototype A clickable mock-up of a product used to test an idea with real people before building it fully. Example: a Figma prototype of an app.
Responsive design A page layout that adjusts to any screen size, from phone to laptop, so it works well everywhere. Example: this site's menu wraps on small screens.

Accessibility a11y Designing so everyone can use a product, including people who use screen readers, keyboards only, captions or high-contrast text. Often required by law and good for everyone. Example: adding alt text to images.
Front end The part of a website or app people see and use, built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
Back end The behind-the-scenes part that stores data, runs logic and talks to other systems, usually on a server. Example: a database that saves orders.
Full stack Working on both the front end and the back end of an application.
HTML HyperText Markup Language The language that defines the structure of a web page: headings, paragraphs, links and images.
CSS Cascading Style Sheets The language that controls how a web page looks: colors, fonts, spacing and layout.
JavaScript The programming language that makes web pages interactive, such as search boxes, calculators and menus.
Domain name The readable address of a website, such as example.com, that you register and renew each year.
DNS Domain Name System The internet's phone book. It turns a domain name into the server address where the site lives.
Hosting The service that stores a website's files and delivers them to visitors. Static sites can often be hosted free, as this one is on GitHub Pages.
HTTPS The secure version of the web's connection. The padlock in the address bar means data between you and the site is encrypted.
A/B test Showing two versions of something (an ad, a page, an email) to different people to see which performs better. Example: two ad videos, compare clicks.
Conversion rate The share of visitors who take the action you want, such as signing up or buying. Conversions divided by visitors. Example: 5 sign-ups from 100 visitors is 5%.
Generative AI AI that creates new content, such as text, images, audio, video and code, from a prompt. Example: FLUX 3 making a video from a sentence.
Machine learning ML A way of building software that learns patterns from examples instead of following hand-written rules. Example: a spam filter trained on labeled emails.
Neural network A model made of layers of connected math units, loosely inspired by the brain. Most modern AI is built on them.
Multimodal A model that can handle more than one kind of input or output, such as text, images, audio and video.

RAG Retrieval-Augmented Generation Letting an AI look up your own documents before it answers, so replies are grounded in real sources instead of memory alone. Example: a chatbot that answers from a company's policy manual.
Training data The examples a model learns from. The quality, variety and rights of this data shape what the model can do.
Bias When an AI treats groups unfairly or gives skewed answers because of patterns or gaps in its training data.
Deepfake AI-made or AI-edited media that makes it look like a real person said or did something they did not. Example: never post one without permission and clear labeling.
Guardrails Rules and checks that keep an AI system within safe, intended behavior.
Human in the loop A design where a person reviews or approves an AI's work before it takes effect. Example: an agent approves each AI-written client email before it is sent.
Agile A way of working in short cycles: build a little, get feedback, adjust. The opposite of planning everything up front.
Scrum A popular Agile method with fixed-length work cycles (sprints), regular check-ins and clear roles.
Sprint A short, fixed period (often one to four weeks) in which a team finishes a set of planned work.
User story A one-sentence request from the user's point of view: 'As a member, I want to add a prompt so I can share what works.'
Stakeholder Anyone affected by or interested in a project, such as customers, managers, members or investors.
Product-market fit PMF When a product clearly solves a real problem for a group of customers who want it enough to keep using and recommending it.
Pivot A significant change of direction for a startup after learning that the first idea is not working.
Bootstrapping Building a business with your own money and revenue instead of outside investment.
Burn rate How much cash a company spends each month beyond what it earns. Divide cash on hand by burn rate to get runway.
Runway How many months a company can keep operating before it runs out of cash.
Churn The share of customers who stop buying or cancel in a period. Lower is better.
CAC Customer Acquisition Cost What it costs, on average, to win one new customer, including marketing and sales.
LTV Lifetime Value The total profit you expect from a customer over the whole relationship. Healthy businesses earn much more per customer (LTV) than they spend to win one (CAC).
Gross margin Revenue minus the direct cost of delivering the product, shown as a percentage of revenue.
Scalability How well a business or system handles growth without costs or problems growing just as fast. Example: a static website serves 10 or 10,000 visitors at about the same cost.
Business intelligence BI Tools and practices that turn company data into reports and dashboards people use to make decisions.
Dashboard A single screen that shows key numbers and charts so you can see how things are going at a glance.
Data warehouse A central database built for reporting and analysis, combining data from many systems.
ETL Extract, Transform, Load Pulling data out of source systems, cleaning and reshaping it, and loading it somewhere you can analyze it.
Data governance The rules for who owns data, who can use it, how accurate it must be and how it is protected.
SDLC Software Development Life Cycle The stages of building a system: plan, analyze, design, build, test, deploy and maintain.
DevOps Practices that bring software development and IT operations together to release updates quickly and reliably.
CI/CD Continuous Integration and Delivery Automatically testing and releasing changes every time someone updates the code. A GitHub Action that checks every pull request is one example.
Technical debt The future cost of quick shortcuts in code or systems. Like borrowing time now that must be repaid later.
Cybersecurity Protecting systems, networks and data from attack, theft and damage.
Encryption Scrambling data so only someone with the right key can read it.
MFA Multi-Factor Authentication Logging in with more than a password, such as a code on your phone. One of the simplest ways to protect an account.
Phishing A fake message or site designed to trick you into giving up passwords, money or data. Example: an email that looks like your bank asking you to log in.
Latency The delay between asking for something and getting a response. Lower latency feels faster.
Data pipeline An automated path that moves data from where it is created to where it is stored and used.
Open data Data that anyone can access and reuse, often published by governments or research groups.
CEO Chief Executive Officer The top leader. Sets vision and strategy and answers to the board.
CIO Chief Information Officer Runs the company's information systems and technology: software, data, security and IT operations. This is a core Information Systems career path.

CTO Chief Technology Officer Leads building the company's technology and product. In a startup the CTO often leads engineering. CIO usually runs internal systems; CTO usually builds what customers use.

CCO Chief Compliance / Commercial / Creative Officer (depends on company) The letters change by industry. In insurance and finance it is usually Compliance (follows laws and regulations). In sales-focused firms it may be Commercial (revenue). Some companies use it for Creative or Customer . Always check which one a company means.
CFO Chief Financial Officer Runs money: budgets, reporting, fundraising, investor relations.
COO Chief Operating Officer Runs day-to-day operations and makes the strategy actually happen.
CMO Chief Marketing Officer Leads brand, marketing and growth.
CAIO Chief AI Officer A newer role guiding how a company adopts and governs AI.
CISO Chief Information Security Officer Protects company data and systems from threats.
C-suite The group of top executives whose titles start with 'Chief'.
VP / Director Senior managers who sit below the C-suite and run departments.
PM Product Manager Decides what to build and why, working with engineers and designers.
KPI Key Performance Indicator A number that shows whether you are winning, such as leads per week.
ROI Return on Investment What you gain compared to what you spent.
MVP Minimum Viable Product The simplest version you can launch to test an idea.
B2B / B2C Business-to-Business / Business-to-Consumer Who your customer is: other companies or individuals.
SaaS Software as a Service Software you rent monthly instead of buying (Notion, CapCut Pro).
CRM Customer Relationship Management Software that tracks leads, clients and conversations.
ERP Enterprise Resource Planning Big systems that run finance, inventory, HR and operations together.
Compliance Following the laws, regulations and rules for your industry.
PE firm Private equity firm An investment firm that buys and improves companies.
Venture capital (VC) Investors who fund early-stage startups in exchange for ownership.
TAM Total Addressable Market The total revenue possible if you won every customer in your market.
Unit economics Whether you make money on each customer after the costs of getting and serving them.

Frontend Front end The part of a website or app you see and touch: layout, buttons, colors, text. It runs in your browser or phone. Business view: it is the storefront. This club site is almost all frontend (HTML, CSS, JavaScript).

Backend Back end The part you do not see: servers, databases and logic that store data, check logins and do the work. Business view: the warehouse, accounting and staff behind the storefront. An AI chat app's frontend is the chat box; the backend sends your message to the model and returns the answer.
Server A computer that is always on and answers requests from other computers, such as sending a web page or running an AI model. 'The cloud' mostly means servers owned by someone else that you rent.
Client The device or app that asks a server for something, like your browser or phone. Client and server work as a pair.

Authentication Authn, login Proving who you are (password, code, fingerprint). Authorization is different: it decides what you are allowed to do once you are in. AI agents need both, so they can only touch what you permit.
Two-factor authentication 2FA, MFA A second proof besides your password, such as a code on your phone. It stops most account takeovers. Turn it on for GitHub, email and any AI account.
Environment variable Env var, .env A setting stored outside your code, often used for secrets like API keys. The file is usually named .env and should be listed in .gitignore so it is never uploaded.
.gitignore A file that lists what Git must not upload, such as .env files and large temporary files. It protects secrets.
Open source Software whose code is public and can be used or changed under a license. Open-weight AI models are a close cousin. Always read the license before using something commercially.

License LICENSE file The file that tells others what they may do with your project. MIT is a common permissive choice: use and change it freely, keep the credit, no warranty. Without a license, the default is that nobody may reuse your work.
Integration Connector A link that lets two systems exchange data, like an AI agent reading your calendar. Each integration needs permissions and creates risk, so connect only what you need.
Webhook An automatic message one system sends to another when something happens, such as 'new order received.' It is how many automations trigger without you checking.
Cache Caching A saved copy of something so it loads faster next time. If you change a website and still see the old version, your browser cache is the usual reason: hard refresh.
Deployment Deploy Putting a finished version live where users can reach it. GitHub Pages deploys this site each time a change is merged.
Uptime The share of time a system is working. Businesses promise it in service agreements, for example 99.9%.
Backup A separate copy of data kept in case the original is lost or damaged. Version control helps for code, but important data still needs its own backup.
Logging and audit trail Audit log A record of who did what and when. It is how you review what an AI agent did and how companies prove compliance.
Least privilege Give a person or AI only the access it needs to do the job, and nothing more. The most important safety rule for AI agents and connected apps.
Scheduled task Cron job, recurring task A job that runs by itself on a schedule, such as 'every morning at 7, search for news and summarize it.' See the scheduled tasks guide.
Virtual machine VM A computer simulated inside another computer. Some AI agents get their own private VM in the cloud to browse and run tasks, kept apart from other users.
Rate limit A cap on how many requests you can send in a time period. Free AI tiers and APIs use them to control cost and prevent abuse.

Business toolkit Using AI safely in a business AI saves real time, but the mistakes are expensive: leaked client data, wrong facts, broken rules. This page is a practical checklist. General guidance for learning. It is not legal advice. Rules differ by industry and change, so check with your compliance contact, your carrier or company policy, and an attorney when it matters. Can I paste this into an AI tool? What are you about to paste or upload? Choose one... Public information (a public web page, a published article) My own draft writing or ideas Internal business information (pricing, plans, strategy) Someone else's full article, book chapter or paid report Client or customer names and contact details Health or medical information about a person Account numbers, Social Security or ID numbers Passwords, API keys or login tokens A real person's photo, voice or likeness The seven rules Protect private data. Treat anything you paste as leaving your control until you know the tool's data policy. Personal and client information, health details, financial identifiers and credentials should stay out unless your organization has approved the tool for that use. Know the tool's data settings. Check whether your chats can be used to train models, how long they are kept, and whether a business plan gives stronger protection. Policies change, so read the current one. Verify before you trust. AI can state wrong facts with total confidence (a hallucination). Check names, numbers, dates, prices and legal or medical claims against an official source. Keep a human responsible. A person should review anything that goes to a customer, regulator or the public. "The AI wrote it" is not a defense. Be honest about AI. Follow each platform's rules for labeling AI-made content. Never present an AI video as a real testimonial, a real event or a real person. Respect other people's rights. Do not recreate a real person's face or voice without permission. Use only music, images and text you have the right to use, and summarize instead of copying. Follow the industry rules. Advertising and marketing rules apply no matter how the content was made. In regulated fields such as insurance, health and finance, get content approved the same way you would for anything else. Examples by situation Insurance agent Fine: ask AI to explain a general concept in plain language. Not fine: paste a client's name, health conditions or policy numbers. Medicare and other plan marketing is regulated, so run any AI-written ad or script through your normal approval process. Marketing team Fine: draft ad ideas and storyboards. Check every claim is true and provable, label AI content where required, and never show a fake customer as if it were real. Student Fine: use AI to explain, quiz and brainstorm. Check your school's policy on disclosure, never submit AI text as your own if rules forbid it, and verify every fact and source it gives you. Before you publish or send: a 60-second check No private or client information is in it. I checked every fact, number and name against a real source. I own or have rights to every image, clip, voice and song. AI use is labeled where the platform or my field requires it. The claims would hold up if someone challenged them. The right person approved it, if my field needs approval. Why it matters for business Data privacy, accuracy and accountability are the same questions an IT or risk team asks about any system. Companies are writing AI policies now, and knowing the basics makes you more useful on day one. Full walkthrough: train your first model in about an hour 1. The idea in business terms A model is a pattern-finder. You show it many past examples with the right answers (for example, leads and whether they became clients). It learns what separates the groups, then predicts new cases. The quality of your data matters more than the fancy part. 2. Pick a small, real question Good beginner questions have a yes/no or category answer and data you can put in a spreadsheet: Will this lead become a client? Is this review positive or negative? Which category does this support email belong to? 3. Build a tiny dataset Open Google Sheets. Make columns for what you know (such as calls made, emails opened) and one final column with the answer (1 for yes, 0 for no). Use at least 50 to 100 rows. More is better. The most important line is the split: you must test on rows the model never saw, or the score is meaningless. 5. Judge the result honestly Compare the accuracy to a simple guess. Write a short README: the question, the data source, the accuracy, and the limits. Optionally upload the model to Hugging Face with a model card. Link both on your resume.
